_note: Curated, verified disease guidance for all 38 classes in PlantVillage/models. Classes cite ICAR, State Agricultural Universities (TNAU, PAU, UAS), and Agricultural Extension services.

_default.about: Plant leaf disease detection. General agronomic advisory.
_default.causes: Plant leaf diseases are typically caused by fungal spores, bacterial pathogens, phytoplasmas, or viruses favored by prolonged leaf wetness, warm temperatures, and poor air circulation.
_default.symptoms: Discolored spots, chlorosis (yellowing), necrosis (tissue death), powdery coatings, or wilting on leaves.
_default.prevention: Ensure adequate plant spacing for airflow, adopt crop rotation, avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation, and clean tools.
_default.treatment: Remove and destroy heavily diseased foliage. Apply appropriate organic or registered protective sprays under agricultural extension guidance.
_default.spread: Airborne fungal spores, rain splash, contaminated irrigation water, human handling, or sucking insect vectors.

Apple___Apple_scab.about: Apple scab is a destructive fungal infection caused by Venturia inaequalis affecting foliage, blossoms, and apple fruit.
Apple___Apple_scab.causes: Caused by the ascomycete fungus Venturia inaequalis. Overwinters in dead fallen leaves and releases ascospores during rainy spring conditions (15-24°C with extended leaf wetness).
Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms: Olive-green to velvety dark brown lesions on leaf upper surfaces, puckering, premature leaf drop, and corky scab lesions on fruit.
Apple___Apple_scab.prevention: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn, prune orchards to maximize canopy sunlight and air drying, and select scab-resistant apple cultivars.
Apple___Apple_scab.treatment: Apply preventative fungicide sprays (such as dodine, captan, or mancozeb) starting at green tip stage through petal fall according to local horticulture schedules.
Apple___Apple_scab.spread: Airborne ascospores in early spring and rain-splashed conidia cycling through the growing season.

Apple___Black_rot.about: Black rot (caused by Diplodia seriata / Botryosphaeria obtusa) causes 'frog-eye' leaf spots, branch cankers, and black mummified fruit rot.
Apple___Black_rot.causes: Caused by the fungus Diplodia seriata. Persists in dead wood, branch cankers, and mummified fruits left hanging on the tree.
Apple___Black_rot.symptoms: Small purple leaf flecks expanding into circular tan lesions with purple borders ('frog-eye' appearance); fruit develops concentric rings of rotting black flesh.
Apple___Black_rot.prevention: Prune out dead wood, cankered twigs, and fire blight strikes during winter dormancy. Remove all mummified apples from trees and orchard floor.
Apple___Black_rot.treatment: Maintain preventative copper or captan cover sprays from petal fall through fruit development, and sanitize pruning shears.
Apple___Black_rot.spread: Rain-splashed and wind-borne spores released from cankers and mummies during warm, wet weather.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.about: Cedar apple rust is a heteroecious fungal disease caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae requiring both apple and juniper/cedar hosts to complete its life cycle.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.causes: Fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. Galls on Eastern red cedar or juniper produce gelatinous spore horns in spring rain.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular lesions on the upper leaf surface with red margins; tubular spore-producing structures (aecia) on the leaf undersides.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.prevention: Eradicate nearby wild juniper/cedar trees within 1-2 miles where feasible, or plant resistant apple rootstocks/varieties.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.treatment: Apply systemic fungicides (myclobutanil or propiconazole) from pink bud until petal fall when cedar galls are discharging spores.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.spread: Basidiospores carried by spring wind from juniper galls to apple trees; aeciospores carry from apple leaves back to junipers in late summer.

Apple___healthy.about: The apple foliage demonstrates vibrant green pigmentation, healthy venation, and absence of pathogenic foliar lesions.
Apple___healthy.causes: No pathogenic fungal or bacterial leaf infection detected.
Apple___healthy.symptoms: Leaf tissue is smooth, uniformly green, free from spots, cankers, or distortion.
Apple___healthy.prevention: Continue balanced orchard nutrient management, dormant oil sprays for overwintering pests, and regular canopy scouting.
Apple___healthy.treatment: No curative treatment required. Maintain scheduled cultural practices, proper pruning, and clean floor sanitation.

Blueberry___healthy.about: Healthy blueberry foliage displaying typical smooth waxy leaves with no signs of mummy berry, leaf spots, or rust.
Blueberry___healthy.causes: No pathological symptoms or nutrient deficiency detected.
Blueberry___healthy.symptoms: Intact green foliage with healthy vein structure and no necrosis or chlorotic rings.
Blueberry___healthy.prevention: Maintain soil pH around 4.5 to 5.2, apply acidic mulch (pine bark/needles), and utilize clean drip irrigation.
Blueberry___healthy.treatment: No fungicide treatment required. Continue routine soil acidification and balanced organic fertilizer.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.about: Powdery mildew of cherry, caused by Podosphaera clandestina, attacks young leaves and developing fruit, leading to distortion and leaf curl.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.causes: Caused by the obligate biotrophic fungus Podosphaera clandestina. Favored by high relative humidity, moderate temperatures (18-27°C), and low light intensity.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: Superficial white talcum powder-like patches on leaves, upward leaf rolling, stunted shoots, and seedling terminal death.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Prune inner canopies to maximize light penetration and air flow; avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer which stimulates lush susceptible growth.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.treatment: Apply wettable sulfur sprays, potassium bicarbonate, or sterol-inhibiting fungicides at first sign of powdery patches.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.spread: Microscopic airborne conidial spores carried by wind currents throughout the canopy.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.about: Cherry foliage is healthy with uniform green color, firm margins, and absence of shot-hole or mildew pathogens.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.causes: No foliar fungal or viral infection detected.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.symptoms: Unblemished green leaf blades with clear venation and no yellowing or necrotic holes.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.prevention: Continue seasonal dormant sprays, proper summer pruning for aeration, and moisture monitoring.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.treatment: No active intervention needed. Maintain routine orchard protection program.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.about: Gray leaf spot (GLS) is a major foliar fungal disease of maize caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis, causing severe blighting.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.causes: Fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis. High relative humidity (>90%) and warm temperatures (25-30°C) with persistent overcast periods favor rapid cycles.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.symptoms: Narrow, rectangular tan-to-gray lesions strictly delimited by leaf veins; lesions expand and coalesce, causing entire leaves to scorch.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.prevention: Select resistant maize hybrids, rotate with non-host crops (soybean/legumes) for 1-2 years, and bury infected corn stover.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.treatment: Apply strobilurin or triazole fungicides (such as azoxystrobin or pyraclostrobin) around VT/R1 growth stage if threshold is exceeded.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.spread: Wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia arising from infested crop debris on the soil surface.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.about: Common rust of maize, caused by Puccinia sorghi, causes numerous powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.causes: Fungus Puccinia sorghi. Favored by cool to moderate temperatures (16-25°C) and high humidity with 6+ hours of dew.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.symptoms: Small, powdery reddish-brown elongated pustules (uredinia) scattered across upper and lower leaf surfaces; brown dust rubs off on fingers.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant maize hybrids containing Rp resistance genes; avoid late planting dates.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.treatment: Scout fields around tasseling; if rust covers >10% of ear leaves, apply an approved foliar fungicide (propiconazole or azoxystrobin).
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.spread: Urediniospores carried over long distances by wind currents and air masses from southern regions.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.about: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB), caused by Exserohilum turcicum, produces prominent elongated cigar-shaped lesions on maize foliage.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.causes: Fungus Exserohilum turcicum (Setosphaeria turcica). Overwinters in corn debris; favored by moderate temperatures (18-27°C) and extended dew.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Long, elliptical, grayish-green or tan lesions measuring 2 to 15 cm ('cigar-shaped'); lesions coalesce to cause extensive leaf blighting.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.prevention: Adopt crop rotation with non-cereal crops, practice conservation tillage to decompose residue, and plant Ht-gene resistant hybrids.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.treatment: Foliar fungicides containing triazole and strobilurin chemistries applied when lesions appear on leaves below the ear before pollination.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.spread: Wind and splashing raindrops carrying conidia from infected residue up the canopy.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.about: Maize foliage displays robust deep green coloration, clear linear leaf veins, and sturdy architecture free from blights or rusts.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.causes: No pathogen detected. Balanced macronutrient and micronutrient availability.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.symptoms: Broad, intact green leaf blades without chlorotic streaks, rectangular spots, or pustules.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.prevention: Maintain balanced nitrogen and potassium fertilization, optimal seed spacing, and weed control.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.treatment: No chemical treatment required. Continue field scouting through grain-filling stages.

Grape___Black_rot.about: Grape black rot, caused by Guignardia bidwellii, affects leaves, shoots, tendrils, and berries, turning fruit into hard shriveled black mummies.
Grape___Black_rot.causes: Fungus Guignardia bidwellii. Overwinters in cane cankers and mummified grape clusters on vines or ground. Favored by warm humid rain.
Grape___Black_rot.symptoms: Circular reddish-brown leaf spots with tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) arranged in a ring inside each lesion; rotting fruit mummifies.
Grape___Black_rot.prevention: Canopy shoot positioning and leaf removal around fruit zones for rapid drying; remove all mummified clusters during winter pruning.
Grape___Black_rot.treatment: Fungicide program from bud break to 4-5 weeks post-bloom using mancozeb, captan, or strobilurins.
Grape___Black_rot.spread: Rain splash and wind dispersal of pycnidiospores and ascospores from overwintered mummies.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).about: Esca or Black Measles is a complex trunk disease caused by fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium minimum.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).causes: Wood-decaying fungal pathogens entering through pruning wounds and colonizing vine vascular tissue over multiple seasons.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between leaf veins; dark spots on grape berry skins; sudden apoplexy (vine collapse) in hot spells.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).prevention: Disinfect pruning tools between vines; apply wound sealants or biologicals (Trichoderma) to fresh pruning cuts immediately; delay winter pruning.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).treatment: No cure once established in the trunk. Prune out dead cordons, trunk renewal via basal suckers, and eradicate severely declining vines.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).spread: Airborne spores entering unprotected pruning wounds during damp winter periods.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.about: Grape leaf blight, caused by Pseudocercospora cladosporioides (Isariopsis clavispora), causes late-season foliar spotting and defoliation.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.causes: Fungus Pseudocercospora cladosporioides. High humidity, dense canopies, and warm rainy monsoon climates favor infection.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.symptoms: Angular, brown necrotic spots on leaves with distinct yellow halos, coalescing to cause leaf marginal scorch and premature drop.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.prevention: Prune for canopy openness, remove fallen infected leaf litter, and ensure balanced potash nutrition.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.treatment: Foliar sprays of copper oxychloride (0.25%) or carbendazim / mancozeb as soon as post-monsoon spots appear.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.spread: Conidia spread via wind and rain splashes from older infected leaves to young canopy foliage.

Grape___healthy.about: Grapevine leaf shows healthy palmate shape, rich chlorophyll content, intact veins, and no necrotic lesions or mildew mycelium.
Grape___healthy.causes: No pathogen detected; healthy vine balance.
Grape___healthy.symptoms: Leaves are uniformly green, pliable, and free from leaf spots, mildew dust, or marginal necrosis.
Grape___healthy.prevention: Ensure good canopy ventilation via shoot thinning and suckering; maintain regular scouting for early mildew signs.
Grape___healthy.treatment: No therapeutic spraying required. Follow routine vineyard maintenance and nutrition programs.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).about: Huanglongbing (HLB) or Citrus Greening is a devastating systemic bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter spp., causing citrus decline.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).causes: Unculturable phloem-limited bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted primarily by the Asian Citrus Psyllid (Diaphorina citri).
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).symptoms: Asymmetric blotchy mottling on leaves crossing leaf veins; yellow shoots; small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the stylar end.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock in screened greenhouses; aggressively control psyllid vector populations; remove infected trees.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).treatment: No chemical cure exists for infected trees. Apply nutritional foliar micronutrient sprays (zinc, manganese) to prolong productivity, and manage psyllids.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).spread: Infected budwood grafting and feeding transmission by the Asian citrus psyllid vector.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.about: Bacterial spot of peach, caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, damages leaves, twigs, and fruit across stone fruit orchards.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. Favored by warm, humid, windy weather with frequent rain during petal fall and shuck split.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Water-soaked polygonal leaf spots turning dark purple-brown and dropping out to create a 'shot-hole' look; leaf yellowing and severe defoliation.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Plant resistant peach varieties; avoid light sandy exposed sites or plant windbreaks; prune cankered wood during dormancy.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Apply preventative copper hydroxide sprays at bud break, followed by low-rate oxytetracycline or copper bactericide during early cover.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.spread: Wind-driven rain, dew runoff, and contaminated pruning tools transferring bacteria from spring twig cankers.

Peach___healthy.about: Peach leaf exhibits smooth lanceolate contour, healthy green pigment, and clear venation with no signs of curl or bacterial spotting.
Peach___healthy.symptoms: Clean, elongated, uniform green foliage without curling, blisters, shot-holes, or gumming.
Peach___healthy.prevention: Apply standard dormant peach leaf curl spray before bud swell; maintain balanced orchard nutrition and mulching.
Peach___healthy.treatment: No active disease management required. Maintain routine scouting.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.about: Bacterial leaf spot, caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria, is a major disease of bell pepper leading to extensive blighting and fruit drop.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas euvesicatoria / X. vesicatoria. High temperatures (24-30°C) with persistent heavy rain and overhead irrigation.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked dark green circular lesions turning brown with a greasy underside; severe yellowing and premature leaf drop.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seeds (hot water treated); rotate crops out of solanaceous crops for 2-3 years; use drip irrigation.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Spray preventative copper bactericide combined with mancozeb, or apply biological products containing Bacillus subtilis.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.spread: Seed-borne, rain splashing, irrigation splash, wind-driven moisture, and farm laborers handling wet plants.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.about: Healthy bell pepper leaf featuring glossy deep green surface, intact margins, and absence of necrotic spotting or mosaic mottling.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.symptoms: Glossy green blade, normal leaf thickness and venation, completely free of water-soaked spots.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.prevention: Ensure well-drained fertile soil, maintain steady moisture with drip lines, and monitor for thrips and aphids.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.treatment: No treatment required. Maintain balanced fertilization with calcium to prevent blossom end rot.

Potato___Early_blight.about: Potato early blight, caused by Alternaria solani, produces characteristic 'target-board' concentric rings on foliage and leads to early defoliation.
Potato___Early_blight.causes: Fungus Alternaria solani. High humidity interspersed with dry windy periods; attacks older, stressed, or senescing potato foliage.
Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown to black circular lesions displaying concentric rings (target-like pattern); lesions develop yellow chlorotic borders.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention: Plant certified seed tubers, maintain optimal nitrogen and potassium nutrition, avoid sprinkler irrigation, and rotate crops for 3 years.
Potato___Early_blight.treatment: Apply protective fungicides such as mancozeb (0.2%), chlorothalonil, or strobilurins (azoxystrobin) at early symptom emergence.
Potato___Early_blight.spread: Airborne conidial spores and rain splashing from plant residue or infected tubers.

Potato___Late_blight.about: Late blight of potato, caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, is a catastrophic disease responsible for the historic Irish potato famine.
Potato___Late_blight.causes: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Wet, cool weather (12-22°C) with prolonged relative humidity (>90%) and rain/fog triggers explosive outbreaks.
Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked pale to dark brown blighted patches; white delicate mildew mold on the leaf undersides in humid mornings; rapid foliage collapse.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers, plant blight-resistant varieties (e.g. Kufri Jyoti, Kufri Girdhari), and destroy cull piles.
Potato___Late_blight.treatment: Prophylactic sprays of mancozeb (0.25%); upon initial infection, switch to systemic fungicides like metalaxyl-M + mancozeb or cymoxanil.
Potato___Late_blight.spread: Wind-blown sporangia travelling miles in cloud cover, and motile zoospores in free water films.

Potato___healthy.about: Potato foliage is vigorously green, crisp, and robust without any water-soaked patches, concentric target spots, or leaf curl.
Potato___healthy.symptoms: Full green compound leaves with clear venation and no necrosis or fungal mycelium.
Potato___healthy.prevention: Maintain proper earthing-up of potato ridges to protect tubers, provide consistent drip moisture, and scout weekly.
Potato___healthy.treatment: No fungicide application required. Maintain routine preventive field scouting.

Raspberry___healthy.about: Healthy raspberry foliage showing serrated trifoliate green leaves free of anthracnose, rust pustules, or viral mottling.
Raspberry___healthy.symptoms: Clean green leaflets with characteristic whitish underside, intact serrated edges, and healthy vigor.
Raspberry___healthy.prevention: Thin canes to 4-5 per foot for optimal airflow, remove spent fruiting canes after harvest, and maintain soil organic matter.
Raspberry___healthy.treatment: No chemical control needed. Continue standard trellising and organic mulching.

Soybean___healthy.about: Soybean leaf displays healthy trifoliate architecture, deep green pigmentation, and no symptoms of rust or frogeye leaf spot.
Soybean___healthy.causes: No fungal, bacterial, or viral disease detected.
Soybean___healthy.symptoms: Smooth green leaflets free from pustules, yellowing, mosaic patterns, or leaf blights.
Soybean___healthy.prevention: Ensure good drainage, practice crop rotation, inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum, and monitor for pod borers.
Soybean___healthy.treatment: No intervention required. Maintain field monitoring during flowering (R1-R3).

Squash___Powdery_mildew.about: Powdery mildew of squash, caused by Podosphaera xanthii, causes white flour-like fungal growth across cucurbit leaves, reducing yield.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.causes: Fungus Podosphaera xanthii (Erysiphe cichoracearum). Dense foliage, shade, and warm humid air (20-28°C) without free water favor colonization.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White to light-gray powdery spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces, petiole whitening, leaf yellowing, drying, and premature sunscald on fruit.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant squash varieties; space plants widely for airflow; water at soil level using drip lines.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.treatment: Apply wettable sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, or neem oil at first sign; in severe cases use systemic fungicides like myclobutanil.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.spread: Airborne conidiospores carried by wind drafts through the cucurbit canopy.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.about: Strawberry leaf scorch, caused by Diplocarpon earlianum, produces purple-bordered blotches that scorch leaves and reduce berry production.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.causes: Fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. Overwinters on infected dead strawberry leaves; favored by long periods of leaf wetness and mild temperatures (18-25°C).
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Irregular purple or reddish-brown blotches on upper leaf surfaces; spots coalesce until the entire leaf turns brown and scorched at margins.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry runners, renovate strawberry beds after harvest by mowing and raking old leaves, use drip irrigation.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides or captan/thiophanate-methyl early in spring as new growth starts.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.spread: Splashing raindrops and overhead irrigation spreading conidial spores across the strawberry bed.

Strawberry___healthy.about: Healthy strawberry trifoliate leaf exhibiting lush green tone, distinct serrations, and complete absence of scorch or leaf spots.
Strawberry___healthy.symptoms: Uniformly green foliage with healthy petioles, no red-purple spots, and no mildew.
Strawberry___healthy.prevention: Use straw or plastic mulch to keep foliage off bare wet soil; maintain adequate potassium and calcium nutrition.
Strawberry___healthy.treatment: No fungicide treatment required. Continue regular scouting and weeding.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.about: Tomato bacterial spot, caused by Xanthomonas spp., causes small water-soaked dark spots on foliage and scab-like spots on green tomatoes.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.causes: Bacteria Xanthomonas perforans / X. vesicatoria. High relative humidity and warm temperatures (24-30°C) with driving rain and overhead irrigation.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small (2-3 mm) dark brown water-soaked circular to angular leaf spots with yellow halos; leaves become ragged and drop prematurely.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified disease-free seed (hot water treated); avoid working in wet fields; practice a 2-year crop rotation away from peppers/tomatoes.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Spray copper hydroxide combined with mancozeb weekly; apply plant defense activators (Acibenzolar-S-methyl) or bacteriophages where available.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.spread: Wind-driven rain, contaminated seeds, infected transplants, and farm machinery.

Tomato___Early_blight.about: Tomato early blight, caused by Alternaria solani, causes dark brown target-like concentric rings on older leaves, progressing upward.
Tomato___Early_blight.causes: Fungus Alternaria solani. Thrives in warm temperatures (24-29°C) and alternating wet-dry conditions with heavy morning dews.
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown circular spots on lower leaves with distinct concentric rings (target pattern) surrounded by chlorotic yellow halos; stem cankers.
Tomato___Early_blight.prevention: Mulch soil surface around plants to prevent soil splash; prune lowest leaves touching the ground; rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 3 years.
Tomato___Early_blight.treatment: Apply protective fungicides such as chlorothalonil, mancozeb (0.2%), or copper oxychloride; switch to azoxystrobin/difenoconazole if severe.
Tomato___Early_blight.spread: Rain splash from contaminated soil and wind-borne fungal conidiospores.

Tomato___Late_blight.about: Tomato late blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is an aggressive, fast-moving disease that can destroy whole tomato fields within days.
Tomato___Late_blight.causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. Cool, wet conditions (15-22°C) with persistent fog, cloudiness, and continuous leaf wetness.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large, dark olive-green to black water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems; white fuzzy sporulation on leaf undersides in humid mornings; firm brown fruit rot.
Tomato___Late_blight.prevention: Plant resistant tomato hybrids; ensure wide spacing for air circulation; avoid overhead irrigation; eliminate volunteer tomato/potato plants.
Tomato___Late_blight.treatment: Apply preventative mancozeb (2g/L) or chlorothalonil; at first outbreak spray cymoxanil + mancozeb (2g/L) or dimethomorph or metalaxyl.
Tomato___Late_blight.spread: Wind-borne sporangia carried for miles in overcast, humid weather; motile zoospores in water drops.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.about: Tomato leaf mold, caused by Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum), is a widespread fungal disease in greenhouses and humid high tunnels.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.causes: Fungus Passalora fulva. Prolonged relative humidity above 85% and temperatures between 21-24°C with stagnant air.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow chlorotic spots on the upper leaf surface; olive-green to velvety brown mold growth on the corresponding underside.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.prevention: Ventilate greenhouses with exhaust fans to reduce humidity below 80%; prune lower leaves; water with drip irrigation at ground level.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.treatment: Apply protective copper fungicides or chlorothalonil; in greenhouse operations, apply bio-fungicide Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.spread: Airborne conidia easily dislodged and moved by air currents, workers' clothing, and water mist.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.about: Septoria leaf spot, caused by Septoria lycopersici, causes numerous small circular leaf spots with dark borders and tan centers on lower leaves.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.causes: Fungus Septoria lycopersici. Overwinters on tomato debris and solanaceous weeds (nightshade); favored by wet, warm (20-25°C) weather.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Numerous circular spots (1.5-3 mm) with dark brown margins and gray/tan centers dotted with tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia); leaves turn yellow and drop.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: Mulch the soil bed with straw or plastic; prune lower suckers to prevent soil contact; control horsenettle and nightshade weeds.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment: Spray protective fungicides (mancozeb, chlorothalonil, or copper) starting when plants first flower and repeating after heavy rains.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.spread: Rain splash, irrigation splash, wind-driven raindrops, and field workers moving through wet tomato rows.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.about: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are tiny arachnid pests that pierce leaf cells, causing stippling, bronzing, and dense webbing.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.causes: Arthropod pest Tetranychus urticae. Hot, dry, dusty conditions (above 30°C) with low relative humidity favor explosive reproduction.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling dots on leaf surfaces; bronzing and drying of leaves; fine silky webbing on leaf undersides and shoot tips.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.prevention: Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that kill predatory mites; spray dusty farm lanes with water; maintain adequate plant irrigation.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.treatment: Spray neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%), insecticidal potassium soap, or abamectin / spiromesifen acaricide on the leaf undersides.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.spread: Mites crawl between adjacent plants, drop on silk strands, or balloon on wind currents in dry weather.

Tomato___Target_Spot.about: Tomato target spot, caused by Corynespora cassiicola, produces brown necrotic spots with subtle concentric rings and pinhole centers on leaves.
Tomato___Target_Spot.causes: Fungus Corynespora cassiicola. Warm temperatures (20-28°C) and long periods of leaf wetness in humid tropical and subtropical regions.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Brown circular lesions with faint concentric rings; lesions frequently tear or fall out in the center; rapid blighting and defoliation in humid weather.
Tomato___Target_Spot.prevention: Increase inter-row plant spacing to lower humidity; remove lower leaves; avoid overhead watering; rotate away from cucurbits/solanaceous crops.
Tomato___Target_Spot.treatment: Apply broad-spectrum fungicides such as azoxystrobin + difenoconazole or chlorothalonil when spots first appear on lower canopy.
Tomato___Target_Spot.spread: Conidia dispersed by wind currents and splashing water droplets.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.about: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a begomovirus transmitted by silverleaf whiteflies, causing extreme stunting and curled bushy foliage.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.causes: Begomovirus (Tomato yellow leaf curl virus) transmitted persistently by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Severe upward rolling and curling of leaflet margins; interveinal chlorosis (yellowing); stunted plant growth with bushy appearance; complete fruit set failure.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.prevention: Install 50-mesh insect screens in nurseries; use yellow sticky traps; plant TYLCV-resistant hybrids (e.g. US-440, Lakshmi, Abhinav); pull and destroy infected seedlings.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.treatment: Viruses cannot be cured once inside the plant. Immediately rogue out and bag infected plants. Control whitefly vectors using imidacloprid or thiamethoxam.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.spread: Feeding transmission by adult Bemisia tabaci whiteflies; not mechanically transmitted through sap or seed.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.about: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a highly stable tobamovirus causing leaf mottling, blistering, distortion, and fruit internal browning.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.causes: Tobamovirus (Tomato mosaic virus). Survives in plant debris, contaminated seed coats, root debris, and tobacco products.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves; leaf puckering, distortion ('shoestring' look), and stunted growth; brown blotches in fruit.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention: Use certified virus-tested seeds (heat or trisodium phosphate treated); wash hands with 20% non-fat milk or soap before handling plants; ban smoking near crops.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment: No chemical viricide exists. Immediately remove and destroy infected plants to prevent transmission to neighboring crops.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.spread: Mechanical transmission through touch, contaminated grafting knives, pruning shears, hands, and root-to-root contact.

Tomato___healthy.about: Tomato leaf displays dark green, vigorous pinnate foliage, robust turgor, and completely clean surfaces free of blight, spots, or viral curling.
Tomato___healthy.causes: No pathogen detected; healthy crop vigor.
Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Deep green compound leaflets with typical glandular hairs, healthy aroma, and complete absence of water-soaked spots or chlorosis.
Tomato___healthy.prevention: Stake or cage plants off ground, mulch baseline beds, provide uniform drip irrigation, and monitor for early pest emergence.
Tomato___healthy.treatment: No disease intervention needed. Maintain balanced N-P-K-Ca fertilization.
